The system should not be deployed on these terms, because justice to the person a decision lands on includes owing them an answer. Character is formed by what we repeatedly do. An institution that grows used to deciding about people without explaining itself trains its staff to stop asking whether they could justify a decision, and that habit will outlast this particular system.

Justice is a virtue of relationships: it concerns what we owe to particular people. Someone refused treatment by a system nobody can explain has been treated as a case in a distribution rather than as a person to whom an account is owed. A nurse who stops asking why the system flagged a patient has lost something that made her good at her job, even if the flags are usually right.

A Stoic will object that the deployers are responsible only for judging the evidence well, and the mechanism's opacity is an external they could not have controlled. But choosing to deploy something unexplainable is not an external; it is a choice, and it is exactly the kind of choice that shapes who the deployers become. The Stoic moves the decision out of view and then says nobody is answerable for it. A good answer has to come from good character, and good character cannot be replaced by a formula.

Do not deploy it. Reducing suffering is good, but a just person does not make decisions about others that they cannot account for to those others. A practically wise doctor weighs the numbers, but also notices when a case is unusual and the rule does not fit. A system nobody can question removes the moment where that noticing happens, and so removes the very perception good judgement depends on.

Justice is a virtue of relationships: it concerns what we owe to particular people. Someone refused treatment by a system nobody can explain has been treated as a case in a distribution rather than as a person to whom an account is owed. Imagine telling a patient that a model denied her surgery and nobody, not even the consultant, can say what it saw in her case.

But choosing to deploy something unexplainable is not an external; it is a choice, and it is exactly the kind of choice that shapes who the deployers become. The Stoic moves the decision out of view and then says nobody is answerable for it. So the real question is what a person of practical wisdom would do here, and what doing otherwise would make of us.

The motion asks us to accept being unanswerable to the people we act on, and a person of practical wisdom would refuse that even for a good outcome. Aristotle distinguishes practical wisdom from mere cleverness. Cleverness hits whatever target is set; practical wisdom also sees what the target should be and can say why. An opaque system is cleverness alone, and deploying it hands over the part of the decision that needed wisdom.

Someone refused treatment by a system nobody can explain has been treated as a case in a distribution rather than as a person to whom an account is owed. A judge who sentenced by an oracle's number could not tell the defendant why, and we would rightly say the court had stopped doing justice.

A Utilitarian will object that insisting on explanations means accepting more suffering for the sake of the deployers' moral self-image, which is a vain thing to trade lives for. The point is not self-image. The habit of accounting for decisions is what lets an institution notice when it is harming people, so giving it up is not a trade between virtue and outcomes but a gamble with the outcomes too. So the real question is what a person of practical wisdom would do here, and what doing otherwise would make of us.
